problem: When VLN agents fail on a navigation instruction, it is unclear whether the instruction, the map topology, or the agent is to blame; there is no systematic understanding of why instructions fail in graph-based, vision-free outdoor navigation evaluation.
motivation: Evaluating instruction quality is confounded by agent-specific artifacts, so failures cannot be cleanly attributed. A principled failure taxonomy and annotated failure traces can guide instruction generation, evaluation frameworks and agent design.
key_idea: Build a four-category taxonomy of navigation instruction failures (linguistic, topological, agent limitations, execution barriers) and an annotated dataset of 492 failure traces from the OSM-based GROKE framework.
insight: Most failures (74.2%) come from agent limitations rather than the instructions themselves, with stop-location errors and planning failures the most frequent subcategories. Evaluation frameworks should therefore separate instruction-quality issues from agent artifacts. Only the abstract was available, so no ablations can be cited.
method: Taxonomy: clusters instruction failures into four categories: linguistic properties, topological constraints, agent limitations, execution barriers, each with subcategories.
Data source: failure navigation traces collected from GROKE, a vision-free evaluation framework using OpenStreetMap graph data.
Annotated dataset: 492 failure traces labeled with taxonomy categories.
Failure analysis: distribution of categories and subcategories across GROKE traces (agent limitations 74.2%; stop-location errors and planning failures most common).

setting.backbone: not specified in abstract (agents evaluated within GROKE)
setting.observation: vision-free OpenStreetMap graph data with text instructions
setting.action_space: graph-based navigation over OSM road/node graph

numbers_note: abstract only; no navigation metrics reported (only the 74.2% agent-limitation share and 492 traces)
results: Of 492 annotated failure traces from GROKE, agent limitations account for 74.2% of failures, the dominant category, with stop-location errors and planning failures most frequent. No baseline comparison is given.
limitations: Analysis is restricted to failures from the GROKE OSM-based vision-free framework, so generalization to visual VLN is unclear.
Dataset is small (492 traces) and covers only failure cases.
